prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form that made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my scientific judgment is unchanged: B019 is the strongest candidate on the shortlist on its merits, not because all six of us ranked it first. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through human GLP-1 physiology and identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, to drugs with independently confirmed effects on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes is complete, mature and stable. Timing is not a concern and no member argued for deferral. The chair's synthesis shows that the remaining disagreement is about the third name and the scope of the citation, not about merit or maturity. I therefore keep a single-part prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, with a citation centred on physiology and the active peptide, which is the discovery step and fits the prize's emphasis on discovery. A second part is not warranted: it would force a split of the GLP-1 names under the three-person limit and would weaken the strongest and best-evidenced part to add a weaker one.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection stands and I do not think it can be argued away. Knudsen's acylated, albumin-binding analogues are what turned the peptide into liraglutide and semaglutide, Habener is outside the credit list yet relevant to the early peptide history, and Mojsov's priority is described by several members as contested. Any trio omits someone with a real claim, and a physiology-framed citation can be read as under-crediting the drug step. Against that, a prize including analogue optimisation would blur discovery and industrial development. The caveat is documented, and I do not think it justifies deferral, since deferring would not make the history any clearer.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treats the acylation and albumin-binding step as a discovery in its own right, and says he would not block Mojsov under a purely physiological citation if the priority question is discussed openly.
responses.response: His openness to Mojsov under a physiological citation narrows our difference to one question: what the citation rewards. I still prefer Mojsov because identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) form is what made both the physiology and the pharmacology tractable, whereas half-life extension is optimisation of a known peptide. I accept his point that the priority question must be discussed openly and not assumed away. The record in front of us cannot settle it, and I would not call the case closed. But an unresolved priority question against Habener is a reason to word the citation carefully around the active form, not a reason to swap in the industrial step. If the committee wants the drug step honoured, it should say so through a deliberate choice of citation, not through the third name.

responses.point: Perlmann supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov but says he would revisit if diligence on Mojsov's priority proves unfavourable, and names B028 (Walter, Mori) as the cleaner two-person fallback if attribution cannot be settled.
responses.response: That conditionality is reasonable and I share it. Our materials cannot establish Mojsov's priority against Habener, so I would want the committee to record that gap openly in the citation wording and not claim certainty. However, I do not think the uncertainty alone makes B028 the better prize. The unfolded protein response is the more self-contained piece of cell biology, but its therapeutic consequences are still emerging, as he and Wahren-Herlenius both note, while B019 has a mature and measured clinical outcome. I therefore keep B028 as an alternative and would turn to it only if the committee concluded that no B019 trio could be defended, which I do not think it has.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius supports a physiology-led B019 and names B014 (CAR-T) or B032 (TNF blockade) as mature, clearly attributable fallbacks if the GLP-1 attribution proves unstable.
responses.response: I agree that B014 is the right fallback if B019 failed, and June and Sadelain remain the cleanest pair there. The design and translational contributions are theirs. I would still leave out Rosenberg, since adoptive cell transfer preceded CAR design, and Eshhar's absence from the credited names remains a gap that is documented and not resolved. I am less persuaded by B032. The Feldmann and Maini chain is strong and mature, but other members find it less original, and no one else ranks it, so I do not see it as a stronger fallback than B014. On her question whether a physiology prize can respect the translational outcome without crediting industry: yes, because the citation can name the active peptide and incretin-based therapies as a consequence without crediting the drug development itself.

responses.point: Sandberg supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with a physiology-and-active-peptide citation, but would revisit if the committee wants the citation centred on the therapy, and asks whether a second part such as B028 would strengthen or dilute the prize.
responses.response: On her second-part question I come down against a second part. Under the three-person limit, adding B028 would require dropping one of the three GLP-1 names, and every one of them has a defensible claim, so the cost would fall on the part we are most confident about. A two-part prize would also add two distinct citations to defend, which does not help a prize whose weak point is attribution. On centring the citation on the therapy, I think that would invite the Knudsen question without answering it, because a therapy-centred citation without Knudsen is internally inconsistent. If the committee does want a therapy citation, the honest configuration is Knudsen in the trio, and I do not think the record justifies that.

responses.point: El Manira supports B019 with Mojsov, keeps B016 optogenetics as an alternative, and asks whether the supplied credit names suffice or whether the case should be deferred until a fuller priority review.
responses.response: I take the deferral question seriously, since a credit list that omits Habener is a legitimate worry. But a documented caveat is enough here. The merit and maturity of the discovery are not in doubt, the committee will not get cleaner primary-record evidence by waiting, and every configuration of the chain leaves someone out. As for B016, I still regard optogenetics as one of the most influential methods in neuroscience, and I take his point about its breadth. But six candidate names for at most three slots, and the open question of separating channel discovery from neuronal application, make it harder to configure than B019. It is not on my alternatives list, which stays with B014 and B028.

uncertainties: Priority among Mojsov, Habener, Holst and Drucker for the active peptide cannot be verified from the supplied record, and Habener is outside the credit list.

Whether the committee prefers a citation limited to physiology and the active peptide or one that reaches the drug step represented by Knudsen; I prefer the former but accept this is a judgment about what the prize rewards.
If B019 had to be set aside, whether B014 (June and Sadelain, with Eshhar's earlier chimeric receptor concept absent) or B028 would be the stronger fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal on any shortlisted ballot is apparent from my profile. I have co-authored with Thomas Perlmann and worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow, and neither relationship involves a shortlisted candidate or a credited name. This is unchanged from round 1, and the chair's summary shows no member requesting recusal. I have not inferred ties from shared institutions or topics.
